meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you don't read the newspaper, you are uninformed. If you do read the newspaper, you are misinformed'?
meta.ogDescription: No—Mark Twain never said it. The Twain attribution appears only c. 1998–2000; the exact wording's author is unknown, echoing Jefferson, Hubbard & Benson.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — a modern aphorism of unknown authorship
answer.authorDates: Wording first documented c. 1998–2000 · falsely pinned on Twain (1835–1910)
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Mark Twain ever wrote or said this. It appears in none of his books, letters, speeches, or the standard compilations, and the earliest attributions to Twain surface only around 1998–2000—nearly a century after his death. As Quote Investigator and the Center for Mark Twain Studies conclude, the exact wording’s creator remains unknown; it appears to have condensed an old sentiment expressed by others.

source.heading: The paper trail
source.excerpt: If you don’t read the newspaper, you are uninformed. If you do read the newspaper, you are misinformed.
trail: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence for Twain and traces the earliest strong match to a 2000 Usenet post in the newsgroup israel.francophones, where it was already being credited to Twain.
The Center for Mark Twain Studies lists it among the “Apocryphal Twain,” noting attributions to Twain do not appear until 1998 or later and became common only around 2007.

The idea is older than the phrasing: Thomas Jefferson wrote in an 1807 letter that “the man who never looks into a newspaper is better informed than he who reads them,” and Mayor Orville Hubbard said in 1955 “it’s better to be uninformed than misinformed.”
source.excerptNote: The line is real and widely circulated—but it is not Twain’s. No primary source in his hand or voice contains it.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identifiable author or first-publication source—it is a modern aphorism of unknown origin, first documented in the late 1990s–2000—so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is definitively not a Twain text (his relevant works are public domain, but this line is not among them).

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain (the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, 1835–1910) was America’s most quotable humorist, author of The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn and The Innocents Abroad. He genuinely spent years as a newspaperman and skewered the press in essays like “Journalism in Tennessee,” which is exactly why a punchy, cynical line about newspapers feels like his—and why it stuck. But feeling Twainian is not the same as being Twain’s: his fame makes him the internet’s single biggest magnet for orphaned quips.

cite.sourceCitation: No authenticated Twain source exists. misattribution.heading: Who really said it?
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Mark Twain” quotes he never said. The wording is a modern compression of a much older grievance about the press; its actual author is unknown, and Twain’s name was attached only decades after his death.

items.why: No instance appears in Twain’s books, letters, speeches, or standard compilations such as Mark Twain Speaking, and it is absent from Barbara Schmidt’s authoritative twainquotes.com. Attributions to Twain surface only from about 1998–2000, per the Center for Mark Twain Studies.

items.scope: An earlier expression of the idea
items.why: Jefferson wrote that “the man who never looks into a newspaper is better informed than he who reads them”—the same sentiment, but not this epigram, as noted by Quote Investigator.

Hubbard said “it’s better to be uninformed than misinformed,” and Benson told BYU in 1979 “it would be better to be uninformed than misinformed.” QI suggests the modern saying likely evolved from such lines—but names no single author.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: not Mark Twain. It is a modern aphorism of unknown authorship—an old complaint about newspapers, distilled into a quip and retro-fitted onto history’s most quotable American, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: The irony Twain might have enjoyed
lead: There is a fitting joke buried in this quote’s history: newspaper columnists spent years citing a fabricated Twain line—in newspapers—to warn readers that newspapers can’t be trusted. An unreliable citation testifying to unreliability is exactly the kind of self-swallowing paradox Twain built careers of humor on.

The sentiment itself is genuinely old. Complaints that reading the press leaves you worse-informed than reading nothing stretch back through Ezra Taft Benson, Orville Hubbard and all the way to Thomas Jefferson in 1807. The phrasing we share today, though, is a late-20th-century coinage—polished, symmetrical, and authorless—that found a famous home it never earned.
context.pull: A fake quote about misinformation, spread by the very medium it mocks.
